title: Certificates on your servers
summary: Ask for a certificate, trust a private CA, renew on time, and keep the key safe, without ever turning the check off.

text: To get a certificate, you send a CA a CSR (certificate signing request): your public key and the names, signed with your key to prove you hold it.
- The private key never leaves your server.
- -noenc: no passphrase, so the server can start alone. On a Mac's LibreSSL: -nodes.
- umask 077: the key is readable by you only, from its first moment (LibreSSL doesn't do it by itself).

$ (umask 077 && openssl req -new -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -noenc -keyout shop.key -out shop.csr -subj '/CN=shop.example' -addext 'subjectAltName=DNS:shop.example,DNS:www.shop.example')
For servers only your team uses, run your own CA, and add its certificate to each machine's trust store.
- Debian only reads files ending in .crt, in PEM.
- curl --cacert lab.crt trusts it for one command, without touching the system.
- Firefox, Node and Python's requests keep their own CA list (NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE).
- Turning the check off (-k) is never the fix: it trusts an attacker's certificate too.
A self-signed certificate is its own issuer: nobody vouches for it, so every client warns.
- Users who click through warnings learn to click through real attacks.
- Let's Encrypt gives free public certificates, renewed by certbot.

scheme: certbot renew ──▶ renews what ends soon
text: Renewing is a program's job, not a calendar's: lifetimes keep getting shorter.
- The certbot package installs a timer that runs certbot renew twice a day.
- A check in your monitoring catches what renewal missed: -checkend gives exit status 1 when the certificate ends within that many seconds.
- The web server must then reload: a script in /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/ runs after each renewal.

scheme: key size      RSA 2048+ or ECDSA P-256
text: A few rules cover most of certificate security.
- Whoever copies the private key can pretend to be your server: guard it like a password.
- Old TLS versions (1.0, 1.1) and old hashes have known attacks: clients refuse them. In nginx: ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
